OccWAM: Occupancy World-Action Models with Joint Scene-to-Ego Flow Matching

Qihang Huang    Wenhui Huang    Collister Chua Affiliation:  Nanyang Technological University, Singapore    Shiyu Fang Affiliation:  Tongji University, Shanghai, China    Zhan Chen Affiliation:  Nanyang Technological University, Singapore    Songyan Zhang Affiliation:  Nanyang Technological University, Singapore    Zhidong Wang Affiliation:  Nanyang Technological University, Singapore    Daiying Tian Affiliation:  Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), Singapore    Chen Lv
Abstract

Occupancy world models provide a structured, metric representation of future driving scenes, making them a promising basis for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing occupancy-aware planners typically couple occupancy prediction and action generation through either hierarchical coupling or parallel multi-task learning. Hierarchical methods use occupancy either as a fully predicted future preceding action generation or as an action-conditioned rollout for trajectory evaluation, whereas parallel multi-task methods predict occupancy alongside planning through a separate branch or auxiliary objective. These interfaces retain either an explicit generation order or a role asymmetry, limiting reciprocal interaction between world prediction and action generation during trajectory formation. We propose OccWAM, an occupancy-native world–action model that jointly generates dense future occupancy and continuous ego trajectories via flow matching conditioned on scene representations. Building on this joint formulation, we introduce scene-to-ego world–action flow matching, a two-stage formulation. The first stage predicts scene-centric occupancy together with an absolute ego trajectory, providing a stable representation of future scene evolution. The same predicted world is then re-indexed into the future ego frames induced by the initial trajectory, where ego motion is represented through adjacent pose increments and a second joint flow refines ego-centric occupancy and motion for action-aligned planning. Unlike video-based world–action models, OccWAM preserves explicit semantic geometry for direct planning reasoning without pixel synthesis. Extensive experiments on Bench2Drive and nuScenes demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in closed-loop driving, open-loop planning, and future occupancy prediction.

1 Introduction

End-to-end autonomous driving has progressed from direct waypoint regression toward planning-oriented structured systems, multimodal generative planners, and vision–language–action models [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. These advances have substantially improved trajectory generation, task integration, and semantic reasoning. Yet a fundamental question remains unresolved: how should an explicitly modeled future participate in action generation?

A growing line of world-model-based policies and world–action models (WAMs) incorporates predictive futures into policy computation. Existing systems range from latent feature alignment and chained world-to-policy architectures to joint video–action generation [6, 7, 8, 9]. These systems show that predicted futures benefit action generation but leave open a representation question: what form should the predicted future take to provide structured and directly usable information for planning?

Existing occupancy-based driving systems instantiate several recurring world–action interfaces. In the action-to-world formulation, candidate actions or intentions are generated, then their future worlds rolled out and evaluated [10, 11]. In the world-to-action formulation, a predictive occupancy representation is constructed before being passed to a downstream planner [12, 13]. Others reduce the sequential dependency via parallel multi-task decoding or ordered discrete world–action token sequences [14, 15, 16]. These formulations retain an explicit generation order, separate output pathways, or discrete prediction sequences. They do not instantiate the interface studied here: dense metric occupancy and continuous ego motion jointly generated through a coupled conditional flow.

Joint occupancy–action generation also introduces a coordinate-representation challenge. Stable world forecasting benefits from a scene-centric frame, where environmental evolution is not entangled with coordinate changes caused by ego motion. Planning, in contrast, benefits from an ego-centric representation that expresses occupied regions relative to the vehicle’s intended local motion. Scene-centric prediction has been shown to separate world evolution from ego-induced perspective changes [17]. World formation and action-aligned reasoning therefore favor complementary rather than identical occupancy representations.

We introduce OccWAM, an occupancy-native world–action model that jointly generates latent future occupancy and continuous ego motion through conditional flow matching. World and Action Experts exchange their evolving states at every transformer layer, allowing predicted occupancy to influence action formation while the current action hypothesis informs future-world prediction. Occupancy therefore participates directly in the generative planning process rather than serving only as a completed planning condition, auxiliary objective, or post-hoc trajectory cost. Unlike video-based WAMs, the generated world retains explicit semantic geometry, supporting direct occupancy supervision and metric planning queries without pixel-space synthesis.

Building on this joint formulation, we propose scene-to-ego world–action flow matching. Stage I jointly generates scene-centric occupancy and an absolute ego trajectory in a fixed current-ego-anchored frame. The predicted world is then re-indexed into the future ego charts induced by the Stage-I trajectory, while the trajectory is converted into adjacent motion increments. This transformed pair forms the structured source of Stage II, which applies a second joint conditional flow in an action-aligned ego-centric representation. Stage I thus models how the world and ego evolve within a stable scene frame, whereas Stage II models how the same predicted world relates to local ego motion.

Both stages share a three-expert Mixture-of-Transformers comprising Understanding, World, and Action Experts. The Understanding Expert provides a frozen semantic context stream, while the World and Action Experts interact bidirectionally throughout both flows. Sharing the backbone across both stages keeps occupancy and action within one unified model.

We evaluate OccWAM on complementary closed- and open-loop benchmarks. Bench2Drive evaluates closed-loop driving under repeated interaction, while nuScenes separately measures open-loop planning and future volumetric occupancy, testing both the generated motion and the fidelity of the predicted metric world.

Our contributions are threefold: (i) We introduce OccWAM, an occupancy-native world–action model that jointly generates dense metric future occupancy and continuous ego motion through a coupled conditional flow, enabling direct bidirectional interaction between world prediction and action generation; (ii) We propose scene-to-ego world–action flow matching. A scene-centric flow first generates future occupancy together with an absolute ego trajectory; the predicted world is then re-indexed into trajectory-induced ego coordinates and jointly transported with ego pose increments by a second conditional flow; (iii) We instantiate a concrete WAM through layer-wise bidirectional interaction with a shared three-expert Mixture-of-Transformers, following the proposed scene-to-ego world–action flow matching. OccWAM achieves state-of-the-art closed-loop driving performance on Bench2Drive and state-of-the-art open-loop planning and future-occupancy prediction on nuScenes.

2 Related Work

World models and world–action models.

World models predict future observations or scene dynamics for simulation, representation learning, and decision-making: recent work moves toward joint world–action generation in robotics [6, 18, 7]. In driving, predicted futures enter action generation: future volumetric features are forecast to inform planning [12], intention-conditioned latent futures are scored to rank trajectory candidates [11], video-generator latents condition a diffusion planner [8], and perception and planning variables are denoised in a shared diffusion space [19]. Closest to our formulation, DriveWAM trains video and action streams under a joint flow-matching objective over an autoregressive temporal sequence [9], while generative planners model multimodal trajectory distributions without an explicit future world [3, 20]. OccWAM retains the joint objective but replaces pixel-space futures with dense metric occupancy, so the generated world is independently measurable and geometrically aligned with the action it conditions.

Occupancy prediction and planning.

Occupancy represents the future scene on a metric grid, so predictions are evaluated directly in the space where planning constraints live. OccWorld tokenizes semantic occupancy and autoregressively generates future scene and ego tokens [15], OccLLaMA extends this to a unified occupancy–language–action vocabulary [16], and later work improves fidelity and efficiency through dynamic–static factorization [21], rendering supervision [22], and next-scale temporal prediction [23]. Connecting the predicted world to action, a few interfaces recur (Figure 1): rolling out action-conditioned futures and selecting by occupancy cost (a) [10], conditioning a diffusion planner on a forecast world (b) [13], decoding occupancy and trajectory in parallel from shared sparse queries (c) [14], or serializing scene and ego variables into one discrete autoregressive sequence [15, 16]. Each imposes an ordering, separate decoders, or a discretization. Most relevant to us, COME separates environmental evolution from ego-induced coordinate change via ego-invariant scene-centric control features [17]. OccWAM resolves this separation generatively: dense occupancy and continuous ego motion emerge from a single coupled velocity field (d), with the predicted world re-indexed into the frames its own trajectory induces, then refined jointly with the ego motion defining them.

Mixture-of-Transformers.

Mixture-of-Transformers assigns modality-specific parameters while preserving cross-modal exchange through joint attention [24], and couples understanding and action experts in embodied models [25]. Closest to our backbone, AutoMoT connects Understanding and Action Experts through layer-wise joint attention for driving [4], and UniDriveVLA adds a third expert for perception [5]. OccWAM instead makes the third expert a World Expert, which generates the future occupancy rather than parsing the present scene. World and Action Experts jointly parameterize the conditional flows of both stages on a shared three-expert backbone.

3 Method

3.1 Overview

Given the current driving context cc, including sensor observations, ego-motion history, navigation inputs, and benchmark-specific scene context, OccWAM generates a paired future world and ego trajectory. Let TT denote the benchmark-specific number of future horizons. The Stage-I supervision is represented in a fixed scene frame as (OS,⋆,aS,⋆)(O^{S,\star},a^{S,\star}), where OS,⋆={[OS,⋆]k}k=1TO^{S,\star}=\{[O^{S,\star}]_{k}\}_{k=1}^{T} is a dense semantic occupancy sequence and aS,⋆∈ℝT×3a^{S,\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 3} is a cumulative planar ego-pose trajectory. Bench2Drive represents the future world as temporal BEV occupancy, whereas nuScenes uses future volumetric occupancy. A frozen frame-wise occupancy autoencoder maps occupancy to a compact latent space; for a sequence OO, ℰocc​(O)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{occ}}(O) and 𝒟occ​(zo)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{occ}}(z_{o}) denote applying the encoder or decoder independently at every horizon and stacking the resulting frames.

As illustrated in Fig. 2, OccWAM combines an occupancy-native world–action generator with scene-to-ego two-stage flow matching. The generator uses a three-expert Mixture-of-Transformers backbone comprising Understanding, World, and Action Experts. The frozen Understanding Expert supplies semantic driving context, while the trainable World and Action Experts receive the current occupancy and trajectory flow states and exchange their hidden representations at every transformer layer. The two stages reuse the same expert backbone but employ representation-specific occupancy and action velocity heads.

Stage I transports independent Gaussian sources toward scene-centric occupancy and an absolute ego trajectory in a fixed frame anchored at the current ego pose. The resulting trajectory defines the future ego frames used to warp the decoded occupancy and is converted into adjacent pose increments. This transformed pair becomes the structured source of Stage II. The Stage-II occupancy target is instead the dataset’s native future occupancy expressed in the ground-truth ego frame at every future horizon. Stage II then transports a model-induced source containing occupancy prediction errors, warp-induced uncovered regions, and pose misalignment toward a complete ego-centric world–action target without introducing new Gaussian noise.

Throughout, r∈{S,E}r\in\{S,E\} indexes the scene-centric and ego-centric flow representations, respectively. In the SS representation, occupancy and cumulative ego poses are expressed in a fixed current-ego-anchored scene frame. In the EE representation, each occupancy slice is expressed in its corresponding future ego frame, while each action element is the adjacent pose increment, whose translational components are expressed along the fixed axes of a canonical sensor-aligned chart. We reserve t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] for flow time and k∈{1,…,T}k\in\{1,\ldots,T\} for the physical future horizon. The symbol ⋆\star denotes supervision targets, ⋅~\tilde{\cdot} the Stage-I output, ⋅¯\bar{\cdot} the transformed Stage-II source, and ⋅^\hat{\cdot} the final Stage-II output. The operator sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot) denotes stop-gradient.
